common_name: Rubikon Hens and Chicks (Glossy Ruby-Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; established clumps need no winter protection but resent standing water.

directions: Rubikon forms tight, glossy rosettes of deep ruby-red leaves gathered around a small green heart, with color deepening to near-crimson through cool weather and strong sun exposure. Short stolons carry numerous offset chicks away from the mother rosette each season, quickly knitting individual plants into a dense mat. A mature rosette sends up a single stalk of pink, star-shaped flowers before it dies back, while surrounding offsets continue the colony. Grow in lean, sharply drained gravelly soil and keep winter wet to a minimum, since rot rather than cold is the main risk to this hardy houseleek.

common_name: Stalked Aeonium (Wavy-Leaf Gran Canaria Saucer Plant)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix and grow in full sun to light shade; this tree-forming species needs protection from frost and from prolonged summer drought stress.

directions: Stalked Aeonium is among the largest species in its genus, eventually building stout, sparsely branched stems topped with broad rosettes of spoon-shaped, undulating leaves up to seven inches long. Like other Canary Island aeoniums it grows actively through the cool, moist months and rests through summer heat, when watering should be reduced. Mature rosettes bear tall, pyramidal spikes of bright yellow flowers in spring, and each flowering rosette dies afterward while side branches continue the plant. Provide gritty, fast-draining soil, full sun to light shade, and frost-free winter conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root offsets or stem cuttings in gritty succulent mix in full sun; the plant branches freely from the base to form a dense, ground-hugging cushion of small rosettes.

directions: Sims' Aeonium branches repeatedly at ground level to build a dense, low cushion of small, bright green rosettes rather than the taller, single-stemmed form typical of many aeoniums. Each rosette carries strap-shaped leaves fringed with fine translucent hairs and marked with faint purplish lines down the center. In spring, flat-topped clusters of yellow flowers rise just above the foliage, a distinctly mounded profile compared to the more conical flower heads of related species. Because it grows at higher elevations on Gran Canaria than most of its relatives, this species tolerates somewhat cooler conditions but still needs sharp drainage and protection from hard freezes.

planting.note: Grow in shallow pots or rock crevices with gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun; the tiny rosettes are easily propagated from stem cuttings.

directions: Dwarf Aeonium is one of the smallest species in the genus, forming a densely branched miniature shrublet of thin stems tipped with rosettes barely over an inch across. The glossy, Sedum-like leaves are green to yellowish-green with fine reddish striping that intensifies in bright light. In spring, slender stalks carry small clusters of star-shaped yellow flowers well above the foliage. Its diminutive scale makes it well suited to shallow bonsai-style containers or crevice plantings where larger aeoniums would overwhelm the space.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright light to light shade; the fine hairs on the stems and leaf margins are a useful identifying feature of this Tenerife species.

directions: Smith's Aeonium is a densely branched shrublet distinguished from other tree aeoniums by the fine hairs that cover its stems and line its leaf margins. Rosettes up to six inches across carry glossy green leaves marked with faint brownish striping on the undersides. Native to forested slopes of Tenerife, it tolerates more shade than most sun-loving aeoniums and produces yellow, reddish-veined flowers on tall stalks in spring. Give it gritty, well-drained soil, protection from frost, and bright indirect light for the healthiest growth.

planting.note: Pot offsets or leaf cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade, sheltering from direct midday sun.

directions: Natal Gasteria is one of the largest species in its genus, eventually forming broad rosettes of long, tapering, mottled-green strap leaves that can each reach over a foot in length. In habitat it clings to sheer sandstone cliff faces in South Africa's Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, a background that explains its tolerance of shallow root runs and reflected heat. Tall, arching flower stalks carry inflated pink-and-white tubular blooms that attract sunbirds. Provide gritty, well-drained soil, bright filtered light, and the infrequent deep watering typical of gasterias.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets in fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade; shallow, wide pots mimic its native crevice habitat best.

directions: Kouga Gasteria stands out among its relatives for its smooth, almost velvety, powdery blue-gray leaves, a marked contrast to the warty texture typical of most gasterias. Young plants hold their leaves in two opposite ranks before maturing into a looser rosette, with each leaf tapering to a sharp point. In its native gorges above the Kouga River it grows wedged into crevices on sheer sandstone cliffs, conditions best mimicked with a shallow, extremely fast-draining pot. Wild plants flower in summer and are pollinated by sunbirds; keep watering light and increase shade during the hottest months to preserve the glaucous leaf color.

planting.note: Pot offsets in a gritty succulent mix with bright filtered light and moderate summer watering; native to humus-rich rock crevices rather than open ground.

directions: Swartberg Gasteria is a compact species with smooth, triangular, recurving leaves arranged in a loose rosette, known from only a few scattered rock-crevice sites in South Africa's Swartberg mountains. It is the only gasteria native to mesic mountain fynbos, growing in humus-rich pockets on both shaded and exposed rock faces at relatively high elevation for the genus. This unusual origin gives it somewhat better tolerance of cool, damp conditions than most warmth-loving gasterias, though it still needs sharp drainage to avoid rot. Grow in a gritty succulent mix with bright filtered light and moderate watering through the growing season.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets in fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright filtered light rather than harsh direct sun; water carefully to prevent rot in this forest-origin species.

directions: Polished Gasteria forms a stemless rosette of short, triangular, distinctly keeled leaves with a glossy sheen unusual for the genus, punctuated by rows of raised white tubercles along the margins and keel. Grown in strong light, the leaves can flush purple, adding to its appeal among collectors. It is known only from a single locality in Afro-temperate forest near Plettenberg Bay, South Africa, an unusually shaded and moist habitat for a gasteria. In cultivation it prefers bright filtered light rather than harsh direct sun, along with a fast-draining mix and careful watering to prevent rot.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Pot offsets in a shallow container with gritty succulent mix and bright filtered light; sparing water suits this cliff-dwelling dwarf species best.

directions: Ellaphie's Gasteria is a dwarf species whose short, triangular, densely tubercled leaves curve back on themselves, giving mature plants a compact, almost Haworthia-like silhouette. Young plants hold their leaves in two flat ranks before the rosette fills in, with dark green coloring set off by irregular bands of raised white warts. It grows wild only on cliffs above the Kouga Dam in South Africa's Eastern Cape, wedged into crevices with minimal soil. Reddish-pink flowers appear on branched stalks in late summer; in cultivation give it a shallow pot, gritty mix, bright filtered light, and sparing water.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
